tracks.title: Behavioural Observation
tracks.description: Learning to read behaviour carefully: telling an observation apart from an interpretation, weighing disposition against situation, and generating alternative explanations before settling on one.

modules.title: Seeing It From Where They Stand

lessons.title: Observation vs. Interpretation
objectives: Distinguish an observable fact from an interpretation of that fact.
Recognise when a conclusion about someone's motive outruns the evidence.
Generate at least one alternative explanation for an ambiguous behaviour.
teach: An observation is something you directly perceived: a word said, an action taken, a change over time. An interpretation is a guess about what that observation means — a motive, an emotion, or a trait. People routinely skip straight from an observation to an interpretation without noticing the jump, especially when the interpretation feels obvious in the moment. Confusing the two makes you confident in conclusions you haven't actually earned, and makes it harder to notice when you're wrong.

Thinking that if an interpretation feels obvious, it must be an observation. Obviousness is not evidence. Separating the two doesn't tell you which interpretation is correct — it only stops you from mistaking a guess for a fact.

An evidence-based inference is a conclusion that stays as close as the evidence allows, naming what remains uncertain and what else could explain the same facts. Good inference doesn't mean refusing to draw any conclusion — it means matching your confidence to how much the evidence actually narrows things down. It keeps you open to being wrong, which is what lets you actually update when new information arrives.

Treating "I can't be sure yet" as an unsatisfying non-answer rather than the most accurate one available. Holding multiple explanations open takes more effort than picking one, and some situations genuinely call for a decision before all the evidence is in.
lessons.example: A normally talkative colleague becomes quiet after another colleague is praised in a meeting, and looks at their phone for the rest of it. Observable: The colleague spoke less and looked at their phone more, starting right after the praise. Reasonable inferences: Something changed in the colleague's behaviour around the time of the praise. What's uncertain: Why the behaviour changed — the praise is one plausible trigger, but not the only one. Alternatives: The colleague felt overlooked by the praise. The colleague received unrelated difficult news just before the meeting. The colleague was simply distracted by something on their phone, unrelated to the meeting. Further evidence that would help: Whether the pattern repeats around similar praise in the future, or a direct, low-pressure conversation with the colleague.
practicePrompts: Think of something you observed about someone's behaviour today.
State only the observable part in one plain sentence.
Separately, name one interpretation you jumped to, and one alternative interpretation that would fit the same observation.
lessons.apply: Today, when you catch yourself forming a quick read of someone's behaviour, pause and separate the plain observation from the interpretation before acting on either.
lessons.reflect: Think of a recent moment you were confident about why someone did something. Was that confidence based on an observation, or an interpretation you'd stopped noticing as a guess?

lessons.title: Attribution: Disposition vs. Situation
objectives: Distinguish a dispositional explanation for behaviour from a situational one.
Recognise the common pull toward crediting disposition over situation, even when situational causes are plausible.
Apply evidence-based inference when weighing competing attributions.
teach: Attribution is the explanation you give for why someone behaved as they did. Explanations tend to fall somewhere between two poles: dispositional (something about who they are — their character, personality, ability) and situational (something about their circumstances — pressure, context, bad luck). People are routinely quicker to reach for a dispositional explanation of someone else's behaviour than a situational one, especially for behaviour that irritates or confuses them — even when a situational cause is just as plausible, or sitting in plain view. Over-crediting disposition makes you too quick to form a fixed judgment of someone from a single instance, and under-credits circumstances that almost anyone might respond to the same way.

Assuming the dispositional explanation must be right because it fits how the person generally seems. Fitting a prior impression isn't the same as being supported by the evidence in front of you right now. Weighing disposition against situation doesn't tell you which one is correct here — it only stops you from defaulting to disposition without considering the alternative.
lessons.example: A new team member misses an important deadline on their very first project. Observable: The team member did not submit the deliverable by the deadline. Reasonable inferences: Something prevented the deliverable from being completed on time. What's uncertain: Whether the cause was something about the person (poor planning, disorganisation) or something about the situation (unclear instructions, competing urgent requests, a personal emergency). Alternatives: The team member underestimated the scope of the work. The team member received conflicting priorities from two different people. The deadline itself was unrealistic given the information they were given. Further evidence that would help: Whether the pattern repeats on a second deadline where instructions are clear and competing demands are lower.
practicePrompts: Think of a behaviour you recently explained with someone's personality or character.
Ask what situational factors might also explain it.
Consider whether you'd apply the same situational generosity to your own similar behaviour.
lessons.apply: Next time you explain someone's behaviour with a trait, deliberately generate one situational explanation before settling on the trait-based one.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time someone misjudged your behaviour as revealing your character, when it was really about your situation. What would you have wanted them to consider instead?

lessons.title: Confirmation Bias and Alternative Explanations
objectives: Explain what confirmation bias is and how it distorts evidence-gathering.
Practise deliberately generating at least one alternative explanation before settling on a conclusion.
Recognise when a pattern is strong enough to narrow explanations versus when it still calls for more than one.
teach: Once an explanation for someone's behaviour comes to mind, it's easy to start looking only for evidence that supports it. Generating alternative explanations means deliberately coming up with at least one other account that fits the same facts before settling on one. People form an initial hypothesis quickly, often from limited information, and then unconsciously favour evidence that confirms it while discounting evidence that doesn't — a pattern known as confirmation bias. Without deliberately generating alternatives, you're unlikely to notice evidence against your first guess, because you were never looking for it.

Believing that a strong hunch is more likely to be correct because it came quickly. A hunch that formed before much evidence was in isn't more reliable for having arrived first. Generating alternatives doesn't tell you which explanation is actually correct — it protects you from narrowing in on one explanation prematurely, which is a different, earlier problem.
lessons.example: After you give a friend honest feedback on a plan of theirs, they stop initiating conversations with you for a week. Observable: The friend hasn't initiated conversation for a week, starting after the feedback. Reasonable inferences: Something changed around the time of the feedback. What's uncertain: Whether the feedback is the cause, and if so, whether it was the content, the delivery, or the timing. Alternatives: The friend is upset about the feedback specifically. The friend is busy with something unrelated this week. The friend tends to go quiet for a while after any feedback, regardless of its content. Further evidence that would help: Whether the pattern continues past this week, or whether asking directly, without sounding accusatory, gets a clear answer.
practicePrompts: Think of a belief you currently hold fairly strongly about someone.
Ask what evidence would change your mind, and whether you've actually looked for it.
Generate one alternative explanation for the evidence you do have, before concluding you were right.
lessons.apply: Before settling on an explanation for someone's behaviour today, deliberately generate at least one alternative explanation first, even if you end up rejecting it.
lessons.reflect: Think of a belief about someone that you've mostly only seen confirming evidence for. Have you actually looked for evidence that would challenge it?

lessons.title: Putting Observation Together
objectives: Combine observation vs. interpretation, attribution, generating alternatives and evidence-based inference to read one real situation completely.
teach: The first three lessons separated four skills out to learn them cleanly: telling observation from interpretation, checking disposition against situation, generating real alternatives, and holding conclusions to the evidence. A real situation hands you all four at once, unlabelled.

Applying only one of these checks and treating that as a complete read. In practice, a confusing moment with someone usually calls for all four together — what did you actually observe, does the pattern (or its absence) point toward the person or the situation, what else could explain it, and how much does the evidence so far actually support any one conclusion.
None of this requires distrusting every read you ever make of someone — it means matching how confident you are to how much work these four checks have actually done on this particular situation.
lessons.example: A usually talkative colleague goes quiet in meetings specifically, but stays normal one-on-one. Reading this completely: the quietness and its meeting-specific pattern are observable; the distinctiveness points toward the setting, not the person; more than one explanation (discomfort speaking in groups, disagreement, a change in format) is worth holding open; and a direct, low-pressure question is a better next step than confident conclusions from analysis alone.
practicePrompts: Think of a confusing behaviour you've noticed in someone recently.
Separate what you actually observed from what you inferred.
Check whether the pattern points toward the person or the situation, and name at least one alternative explanation.
lessons.apply: Next time someone's behaviour puzzles you, run all four checks together before settling on an explanation: what's observable, what the pattern suggests, what else could explain it, and how confident the evidence actually supports being.
lessons.reflect: Across these three lessons, which single check — separating observation from interpretation, checking the situation, or generating alternatives — do you most often skip?

lessons.title: Does This Pattern Hold?
objectives: Use consistency, distinctiveness and consensus to weigh a dispositional explanation against a situational one.
Recognise when only one of the three checks has been run, and why that's not enough on its own.
Name what remains uncertain even after running all three checks.
teach: Before explaining someone's behaviour, three questions sharpen the picture. Consistency: does this person behave this way in this situation most of the time, or was this a one-off? Distinctiveness: do they behave this way only in this kind of situation, or everywhere? Consensus: would most people behave this way in this situation, or is this person unusual? Together these are often called the covariation approach to reading behaviour.

Jumping straight to "that's just how they are" without checking any of the three. A trait explanation can feel obvious in the moment, but consistency, distinctiveness and consensus are what actually tell you whether disposition or situation is doing the work — skipping them means guessing with confidence you haven't earned.

Low consistency (a one-off), high distinctiveness (only in this specific situation), and high consensus (most people would react this way) together point toward the situation, not the person. High consistency, low distinctiveness (happens everywhere), and low consensus (most people wouldn't) together point toward the person.

Treating one of the three questions as enough on its own. A single "yes" to consistency doesn't settle it — distinctiveness and consensus can still point the other way, and all three need to be weighed together, not picked from selectively.
lessons.example: A team member snaps at a colleague in a meeting. Consistency: this is the third time this month the same colleague has triggered a sharp response from them (high). Distinctiveness: they're calm and easygoing with everyone else on the team (high — only this one colleague). Consensus: no one else on the team reacts sharply to that colleague (low). High consistency plus high distinctiveness plus low consensus points toward something specific between these two people, not a general short temper.
practicePrompts: Think of a behaviour you've recently explained with a trait ("they're just like that").
Ask: does this person act this way in this situation most of the time (consistency)?
Ask: do they act this way only in this kind of situation, or everywhere (distinctiveness)?
lessons.apply: Next time you catch yourself explaining someone's behaviour with a trait, run the three checks — consistency, distinctiveness, consensus — before deciding whether it's really about them or about the situation.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you explained someone's behaviour with "that's just who they are." Would consistency, distinctiveness and consensus have pointed the same way, or somewhere else?

lessons.title: How Common Is This, Really?
objectives: Explain what a base rate is and why it matters when judging a single instance of behaviour.
Recognise when a vivid specific case is being allowed to override a known or estimable base rate.
Use a rough base-rate estimate to judge how much one instance should update a conclusion.
teach: A base rate is how common something is in general, before you look at any specific case. When you're trying to explain one instance of behaviour, the base rate tells you how surprising that instance actually is — a behaviour that's common in general needs less special explanation than one that's rare.

Ignoring the base rate because a specific, vivid detail feels more persuasive. A striking individual case can feel like it overrides the general pattern, but the base rate doesn't stop applying just because one example feels compelling — if anything, vivid cases are often what make people forget to check it.

Ignoring the base rate in favour of specific details is sometimes called base-rate neglect. It tends to produce more confident conclusions than the evidence actually supports, because a single vivid case is treated as if it were representative, when it might be the rare exception the base rate warns you about.

Assuming that because you don't know the exact base rate, it doesn't matter. Even a rough estimate of how common something generally is — rather than ignoring the question entirely — narrows down which explanations are more or less likely.
lessons.example: A new hire makes a mistake in their first week and a colleague says, "they're clearly not cut out for this." If most new hires make at least one mistake in their first week — a high base rate for "new hire makes an early mistake" — this one instance is weak evidence of anything specific about this person. Only if early mistakes were rare in general would this particular case stand out as needing a special explanation.
practicePrompts: Think of a recent case where you judged someone from one instance of behaviour.
Ask: roughly how common is that behaviour among people in that situation generally?
If it's common, does this one instance really say much about this specific person?
lessons.apply: Before concluding something from a single case, ask how common that kind of case generally is — and let that shape how much weight you put on this one instance.
lessons.reflect: Where have you let one striking case overshadow how common that kind of thing actually is in general?

lessons.title: Don't Mistake Drift for an Effect
objectives: Explain regression to the mean and why it follows unusually extreme performances.
Recognise when a change is being credited to an intervention that regression to the mean would predict anyway.
Distinguish a genuine effect from ordinary drift back toward a typical level.
teach: An unusually good or unusually bad performance tends to be followed by one closer to average, just from the ordinary ups and downs of performance — not because anything changed. This natural drift back toward the typical level is called regression to the mean.

Crediting whatever happened right after an extreme performance — praise, criticism, a new routine — as the cause of the improvement or decline that followed. If the change would likely have happened anyway, from drift alone, attributing it to your intervention overstates what that intervention actually did.

Regression to the mean is strongest right after the most extreme performances, since those are the ones with the most room to drift back toward average. A performance that was only mildly above or below typical has much less regression to show.

Concluding that because regression to the mean is possible, no intervention ever has a real effect. The point isn't that nothing works — it's that an improvement following an extreme result needs more than "it followed an extreme result" as evidence before you credit whatever you did in between.
lessons.example: A manager praises a salesperson after an unusually strong month, and the next month's numbers are more typical. The manager concludes the praise "went to their head" and backfired. An equally likely explanation: an unusually strong month was always likely to be followed by a more ordinary one, with or without the praise — regression to the mean, not an effect of the praise at all.
practicePrompts: Think of a time an extreme result was followed by a more typical one.
Was there something — praise, a change, an intervention — that happened in between?
Could the more typical result have happened anyway, just from ordinary drift?
lessons.apply: Next time an extreme result is followed by a more typical one, check whether regression to the mean alone could explain the change before crediting whatever happened in between.
lessons.reflect: Where have you, or someone else, credited an intervention for a change that might have just been regression to the mean?

lessons.title: One Instance Isn't a Pattern Yet
objectives: Explain why a pattern seen in only a few instances is less reliable than it feels.
Recognise when a small-sample pattern is being treated with the confidence of a large one.
Match confidence in a generalisation to how many instances it's actually based on.
teach: A pattern seen across only a few instances is much less reliable than it feels. Small samples are more likely to show an extreme or lopsided result purely by chance, even when the underlying tendency is actually close to average.

Treating a pattern from two or three instances with the same confidence you'd give a pattern seen across many. The feeling of "I've seen this happen before" doesn't track how many times is actually enough to rule out chance.

More observations, across more varied situations, make a pattern more trustworthy. This doesn't mean waiting indefinitely before drawing any conclusion — it means matching your confidence to how many instances you've actually seen, and staying open to revising as more come in.

Assuming that because a small sample isn't fully reliable, gathering more evidence is pointless. More instances genuinely do narrow things down — the error is treating too few of them as if they'd already settled the question.
lessons.example: A friend is late twice in a row and gets labelled "always late." Two instances is a small sample — not nearly enough to rule out two unrelated, one-off causes. A pattern across ten occasions, in different circumstances, would be far harder to explain any other way.
practicePrompts: Think of a general conclusion you've drawn about someone ("they're always...", "they never...").
Count how many actual instances that conclusion is based on.
If it's two or three, what's one other explanation that would still fit that small a sample?
lessons.apply: Before generalising from a pattern, count how many instances it's actually based on — and treat two or three as a reason for caution, not confidence.
lessons.reflect: Where have you generalised about someone from fewer instances than you'd want to admit?

lessons.title: Patterns, Combined
objectives: Combine consistency/distinctiveness/consensus, base rates, regression to the mean, and small-sample caution to judge a pattern over time correctly.
teach: This module's four ideas all govern how much weight a pattern over time actually deserves: the covariation check, how common the behaviour generally is, whether an extreme result is just drifting back to average, and whether enough instances exist to trust the pattern at all.

Treating a developing pattern as settled after checking only one of these. A real pattern — someone's performance, a recurring behaviour, a string of related events — usually needs more than one of these checks as it develops, not a single verdict delivered early and never revisited.

Confidence in a read of a pattern should grow or shrink as genuinely new evidence arrives, not stay fixed at whatever the first instance suggested — that's the thread connecting all four ideas in this module.
lessons.example: A new team member misses an early deadline (low consistency, a plausible situational cause — new tools, a high base rate for that kind of early friction). More misses follow under normal conditions (the pattern strengthens). A good deadline follows feedback (possibly the feedback working, possibly regression to the mean — not yet established). Across four data points total, real caution about a settled verdict on their reliability is still warranted — a small, mixed sample.
practicePrompts: Think of a pattern involving someone's behaviour that's developed over several instances.
Check it against as many of this module's four ideas as apply.
Notice whether your confidence in your read has actually tracked the number and quality of instances.
lessons.apply: Next time you're forming a judgment about a pattern in someone's behaviour, explicitly check it against consistency/distinctiveness/consensus, the base rate, possible regression to the mean, and whether the sample is actually large enough yet.
lessons.reflect: Across this module, which idea most changed how quickly you're willing to call something a real pattern rather than noise?

lessons.title: When Words and Body Don't Match
objectives: Notice when someone's words and nonverbal behaviour conflict, and treat the mismatch itself as worth attention, without decoding the nonverbal cue alone as proof of anything.
teach: Congruence is whether what someone says matches how they say it and how they're behaving while saying it. A flat, hesitant "I'm fine" and an enthusiastic "I'm fine" are the same two words carrying very different information.

Treating a single nonverbal cue — crossed arms, lack of eye contact, a tense posture — as a reliable, standalone signal of a specific feeling. Research on reading isolated gestures this way is weak; a mismatch between words and delivery is worth noticing, but the specific nonverbal cue alone doesn't reliably decode to one meaning.

When words and delivery don't match, the honest response is to notice the mismatch as information worth following up on — not to confidently declare what the 'real' feeling underneath must be, based on the nonverbal cue alone.
lessons.example: A colleague says "no, it's fine, go ahead" in a flat, clipped tone, arms crossed. The mismatch between the words and the delivery is worth noting and maybe gently checking ("you sure? you can say if it's not a good time") — rather than either taking the words at pure face value or confidently declaring, from the crossed arms alone, that they're definitely annoyed.
practicePrompts: Think of a recent moment where someone's words and tone or body language didn't quite match.
Name the mismatch specifically, without jumping to a conclusion about what it 'really' meant.
Consider what a direct, low-pressure check-in might have looked like.
lessons.apply: Next time someone's words and delivery don't match, name the mismatch to yourself and consider a gentle, direct check-in, rather than silently deciding what it means.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time your own words and tone didn't match how you actually felt. What would you have wanted the other person to do about that mismatch?

lessons.title: What Tone and Pace Carry
objectives: Attend to tone and pacing as information in their own right, not just the literal content of what's said.
teach: How something is said — tone, pace, pauses, volume — carries real information alongside the literal words, sometimes more than the words themselves. A rushed, clipped "sure, whatever works" communicates something different from an unhurried, warm version of the same sentence.

Focusing entirely on transcribing what was literally said while missing what the delivery itself communicated. Two people can say the exact same sentence and mean very different things, depending entirely on how it's said.
Tone and pace are still just signals, not certainties — the same caution that applies to any single nonverbal cue applies here too: notice it, don't over-decode it in isolation.
lessons.example: A friend texts "ok" to a plan you suggested. In person, the equivalent might be an immediate, warm "ok!" or a long pause followed by a flat "...ok." The literal content is identical; the pacing and tone (where visible) carry most of the actual information about how they feel about the plan.
practicePrompts: Think of a recent conversation where tone mattered more than the literal words.
Describe what the tone or pace specifically communicated, separate from the words.
Consider a moment you might have missed a tone shift by focusing only on content.
lessons.apply: In your next conversation, notice tone and pace deliberately, as information separate from the literal words, rather than only tracking content.
lessons.reflect: Think of a message or comment you misread because you only registered the words, not the tone. What did you miss?

lessons.title: Knowing Someone's Normal First
objectives: Establish a sense of someone's baseline behaviour before treating a change as meaningful.
teach: A baseline is what's normal for a specific person — their usual energy, talkativeness, tone, expressiveness. A deviation from someone's own baseline is far more informative than comparing their behaviour to some imagined 'typical' person.

Reading a behaviour as significant without knowing what's normal for that person. A naturally quiet, reserved person being quiet today tells you much less than a normally animated person suddenly being quiet.

Building a baseline takes time and repeated observation — with someone you don't know well, there often isn't one yet, which is itself a reason for extra caution before reading much into any one behaviour.
lessons.example: A naturally soft-spoken, reserved coworker gives short answers in a meeting. Without knowing this is simply their baseline, it might wrongly read as disengagement or frustration — compared to a normally talkative colleague suddenly giving short answers, which really would be a meaningful deviation from their own normal.
practicePrompts: Think of someone whose baseline behaviour you know well.
Think of someone you don't know well yet, and notice how much less confidently you can read their behaviour.
Consider a time you misjudged someone because you compared them to a generic 'normal' rather than their own baseline.
lessons.apply: Before reading much into someone's behaviour, check whether you actually know their baseline — and hold your read more loosely if you don't.
lessons.reflect: Think of someone you initially misjudged before you knew their normal. What would knowing their baseline earlier have changed?

lessons.title: The Same Signal, a Different Meaning
objectives: Recognise that the same signal can carry different meanings in different contexts or cultures, rather than assuming a fixed, universal meaning.
teach: The same signal — eye contact, a pause before answering, a direct versus indirect way of declining — can mean different things depending on the setting, relationship, or cultural background involved. There's no single, universal decoder.

Assuming a signal means the same thing it would in your own default context, without considering that the person's background, the specific relationship, or the setting might shape what it actually signals.
This isn't about memorising a list of cultural rules — it's about holding your read of any signal a bit more loosely when context, background, or relationship might reasonably shift what it means.
lessons.example: Direct eye contact reads as confident and engaged in some settings and relationships, and as overly intense or even disrespectful in others. Reading someone's eye contact (or avoidance of it) without considering their context risks applying the wrong decoder entirely.
practicePrompts: Think of a signal you'd normally read a certain way.
Consider a context or relationship where that same signal might mean something different.
Notice how holding the read more loosely changes your confidence in it.
lessons.apply: Before reading a signal confidently, consider whether the person's context, relationship to you, or background might shift what it actually means.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you misread a signal because you assumed it meant what it would mean in your own usual context.

lessons.title: Reading a Moment Completely
objectives: Combine congruence, tone, baseline and context to read a real moment completely, without over-decoding any single cue.
teach: This week covered four pieces of reading a real moment: do the words and delivery match, what does the tone and pace carry, what's this person's normal, and does context shift what any of this means. A real moment hands you all four at once.

Reading one signal confidently — a tone shift, a mismatch, a deviation from normal — without checking it against the others. A tone shift that's actually just this person's baseline isn't a real signal at all; a mismatch that makes sense given the context might not be worth much either.

None of these four checks are about becoming a confident decoder of other people. They're about reading more carefully and more cautiously — noticing more, concluding less, until there's reason to be more confident.
lessons.example: A colleague's reply sounds clipped (tone) and the words say "it's fine" while their usual replies are warmer (baseline) — but you also know they're in a culture and workplace context where directness and brevity is simply the professional norm, not a sign of being upset (context). Reading all four together, rather than any one alone, gives a much more careful picture.
practicePrompts: Think of a real moment with someone recently.
Check it against all four: congruence, tone, baseline, and context.
Notice whether your confidence in your read changes once all four are considered together.
lessons.apply: Next time you're reading a real moment with someone, deliberately check congruence, tone, baseline, and context together before concluding anything.
lessons.reflect: Across this week, which single check — congruence, tone, baseline, or context — do you most often skip when reading someone?

lessons.title: More Than One Cause
objectives: Recognise that a single signal almost always has more than one plausible cause, and resist settling on just one.
teach: Almost any single signal — a sigh, a long pause, a tense jaw — has more than one plausible cause. The same sigh can mean frustration, tiredness, relief, or nothing much at all.

Picking the first, most dramatic-sounding explanation for a signal and treating it as settled, the same error generating alternative explanations (from the first module) was built to catch — now applied specifically to reading signals in the moment.
Ambiguity doesn't mean signals are useless — it means a single signal is a reason to look further (at congruence, baseline, context, or just to ask), not a reason to conclude.
lessons.example: A friend sighs heavily while looking at their phone. That sigh alone could mean they got bad news, they're tired, they're frustrated with an unrelated app, or they're just stretching — treating any one of these as the confirmed explanation from the sigh alone overclaims what one signal can actually tell you.
practicePrompts: Think of a recent signal you noticed in someone — a sigh, a pause, a look.
List at least two different plausible causes for it.
Notice how differently confident you'd feel acting on just one versus holding several open.
lessons.apply: Next time you notice a single signal in someone, generate at least two plausible causes before acting on any one of them.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you acted on a single signal that turned out to mean something completely different than you assumed.

lessons.title: Stress Response or Emotion?
objectives: Distinguish a physiological cause for a signal from an emotional one, rather than defaulting to an emotional explanation.
teach: Many signals that look emotional have a purely physical explanation: fidgeting from too much caffeine, a flat affect from exhaustion, irritability from being too cold or too hungry, a racing heart from having just climbed stairs.

Defaulting straight to an emotional explanation for a physical signal, without considering ordinary physical causes first. Jitteriness, flatness, and irritability all have mundane physical explanations at least as often as emotional ones.
This isn't about dismissing real emotional signals — it's about genuinely considering the physical explanation alongside the emotional one, rather than skipping straight past it.
lessons.example: A normally steady colleague seems jittery and unfocused in a morning meeting. Before concluding they're anxious about something specific, it's worth considering that they mentioned having three coffees before 9am, skipped breakfast, or got very little sleep — all physical explanations at least as plausible as an emotional one.
practicePrompts: Think of a signal you recently read as emotional in someone.
Consider at least one plausible physical explanation for the same signal.
Notice whether you actually checked, or just assumed the emotional read was correct.
lessons.apply: Next time you read a signal as emotional, pause and consider at least one physical explanation before settling on the emotional one.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time your own physical state (tired, hungry, caffeinated) was misread by someone else as an emotional state.

lessons.title: Reading a Room's Shifting Energy
objectives: Notice a shift in a group's collective engagement, based on the pattern across the group, not one person's reaction.
teach: A room or group has its own collective energy — engagement, restlessness, enthusiasm — that's a real pattern across several people, not just one person's individual reaction.

Reading the whole room's mood from a single visible reaction — one person's frown, one yawn — rather than the pattern across the group. One person's individual state doesn't necessarily reflect everyone else's.

Reading a room well means scanning broadly — posture, attention, side conversations, energy level — across several people, the same way a good read of one person combines several signals rather than one.
lessons.example: In a long meeting, one person yawns. That alone says little about the room. Noticing that several people have also started checking their phones, side conversations have picked up, and posture has slumped across most of the table is a genuine read of shifting group energy — the single yawn wasn't.
practicePrompts: Think of a group setting you were recently in — a meeting, a class, a gathering.
Consider the pattern across several people, not just one person's reaction.
Notice what a genuine shift in group energy would actually look like, versus one person's individual moment.
lessons.apply: Next time you're reading a room, scan across several people's engagement rather than anchoring on one person's visible reaction.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you misjudged a whole room's mood based on one person's reaction. What did the broader pattern actually look like?

lessons.title: Checking Your Read
objectives: Verify an inferred read of someone's state with a direct, low-pressure question, rather than acting on the inference alone.
teach: However carefully a read is built — congruence, tone, baseline, context, multiple possible causes considered — it's still an inference, not a fact. A direct, low-pressure question is usually the single most reliable way to actually find out.
Treating a careful, multi-signal read as confirmed and acting on it without ever checking, even when a simple direct question was available and low-cost.
Checking doesn't mean announcing your whole analysis — a simple, low-pressure "you doing okay?" or "how's this landing for you?" usually does the job without putting the other person on the spot.
lessons.example: After reading several signals that suggest a colleague is overwhelmed — tense tone, short answers, a deviation from their normal — rather than quietly deciding to take work off their plate based on the inference alone, a simple "you seem a bit stretched today, everything okay?" actually finds out, rather than guessing.
practicePrompts: Think of a recent read you built carefully from several signals.
Consider whether you ever actually checked it against reality.
Draft a simple, low-pressure question that would have checked it directly.
lessons.apply: Next time you build a careful read of someone's state, follow it with a direct, low-pressure question rather than acting on the inference alone.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time acting on an unchecked read went wrong. What would a simple direct question have told you instead?

lessons.title: Signals, Combined
objectives: Combine signal ambiguity, physiological explanations, group-energy reading and checking your read into one complete approach to reading people.
Describe a real situation, using everything covered across both signal-reading modules.
teach: This week covered holding a signal's ambiguity open, considering physical causes, reading a group rather than one person, and checking any read against reality. Together with last week's congruence, tone, baseline and context, that's eight separate habits for reading people more carefully, not more confidently.

Treating 'reading people well' as becoming a confident decoder. The actual skill this whole module built is closer to the opposite: noticing more, concluding less, holding reads loosely, and checking before acting.

This closes out both signal-reading modules. The next modules build on this foundation — listening, feedback, and perspective-taking all assume you're reading signals this carefully rather than jumping to conclusions from a single cue.
lessons.example: A teammate seems withdrawn in a group meeting — tense tone, short answers, unlike their usual self (congruence, tone, baseline). Rather than reading the whole room as tense from this one person (group energy), considering only an emotional cause while they mentioned a rough commute (physiological), or acting on the inference silently, checking in afterward with a simple, direct question actually finds out what's going on.
practicePrompts: Think of a real, current situation involving reading someone or a group.
Check it against all eight ideas from this week and last.
Consider what checking your read directly would look like here.
lessons.apply: In your next real interaction, deliberately hold your read of someone loosely, and check it with a direct question before acting on it.
lessons.reflect: In your own words, describe a real recent moment of reading someone or a room, and check it against as many of these eight ideas as actually apply.

lessons.title: Giving Someone Your Actual Attention
objectives: Give someone genuine, undivided attention while they're speaking, rather than appearing to listen while mentally elsewhere.
teach: Active listening starts with actually attending — putting down the phone, facing the person, not doing something else at the same time. It sounds obvious, and it's routinely skipped anyway.

Appearing to listen — nodding, making eye contact — while mentally elsewhere: distracted, or already composing what to say next. The other person can usually tell, even when the outward signs look right.

This isn't about dramatic gestures of attentiveness — it's about the basic, unglamorous discipline of actually directing your attention to what's being said, for the length of time it takes to be said.
lessons.example: A friend starts telling you about a hard day while you're half-scrolling your phone, nodding along. Even if you catch most of the words, you miss the parts that would have told you how to actually respond well — and they usually notice the half-attention anyway.
practicePrompts: Think of a recent conversation where you were only half-listening.
Identify what pulled your attention away.
Consider what fully attending would have actually required — not more effort, just removing the distraction.
lessons.apply: In your next real conversation, remove the obvious distraction (phone down, other task paused) before the other person starts speaking, not partway through.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you noticed someone wasn't really listening to you, even though they looked like they were. What gave it away?

lessons.title: Saying Back What You Heard
objectives: Paraphrase what someone said to confirm understanding before responding with your own view.
teach: Paraphrasing is restating what you heard, in your own words, before responding with your own view — "so what you're saying is..." It confirms you actually understood, and shows the other person they were heard.
Skipping straight to your own response or opinion without confirming understanding first. It's easy to respond to what you assumed someone meant, rather than what they actually said.
A good paraphrase isn't a word-for-word repeat — it's a genuine attempt to capture the meaning, which also makes it easy for the other person to correct you if you got it wrong.
lessons.example: A colleague describes a frustrating situation with a client. Before offering advice, saying "so it sounds like the real issue is the client keeps changing requirements after sign-off, not the requirements themselves" confirms the actual understanding — and gives the colleague a chance to correct it if that's not quite right.
practicePrompts: Think of a recent conversation where you jumped straight to a response.
Draft what a paraphrase would have sounded like before that response.
Notice whether your assumed understanding matches what a careful paraphrase would have captured.
lessons.apply: In your next conversation about something that matters, paraphrase what you heard before offering your own view, and notice if it gets corrected.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time someone responded to something you didn't actually say. What would a paraphrase have caught before they responded?

lessons.title: Questions That Actually Open Things Up
objectives: Ask open questions that genuinely invite the other person's view, rather than leading questions that steer toward a particular answer.
teach: An open question genuinely invites the other person's own answer — "what did you think of it?" A leading question presupposes or steers toward a particular answer — "don't you think it went badly?" already contains the expected response.
Asking a leading question while believing it's a genuine, open one. Leading questions often don't feel leading from the inside — they feel like obviously reasonable framings.
The test is whether the question would sound just as natural with the opposite answer implied. "What did you think?" passes; "wasn't that a disaster?" doesn't.
lessons.example: "Don't you think we should just cancel the project?" presupposes an answer and makes genuine disagreement harder to voice. "What do you think we should do about the project?" genuinely opens space for an answer that might be completely different from what was expected.
practicePrompts: Think of a question you've recently asked someone.
Check whether it presupposed a particular answer.
Rewrite it as a genuinely open version.
lessons.apply: Before asking an important question, check it for the leading-question test: would it sound equally natural with the opposite answer implied?
lessons.reflect: Think of a time someone asked you a leading question that made it hard to give your real answer. What would an open version have sounded like?

lessons.title: Listening to Understand, Not to Respond
objectives: Notice and resist formulating your reply while someone is still speaking, so you're actually taking in what they're saying.
teach: It's easy to spend someone else's talking time drafting your own reply — planning what to say next, waiting for a pause to jump in — rather than actually processing what they're saying as they say it.

Not noticing this is happening. It feels like listening from the inside, since attention is still technically directed at the other person, but the processing is going toward constructing a response, not toward understanding.

The fix isn't complicated: notice when your attention has shifted to planning a reply, and bring it back to simply taking in what's being said, trusting that a response will come once they've actually finished.
lessons.example: A friend is explaining why they're upset about something, and halfway through, you've already started composing your defence of the thing they're upset about — so you miss the second half of what they actually said, including the part that might have changed your response entirely.
practicePrompts: Think of a recent conversation where you noticed yourself planning a reply mid-sentence.
Consider what you might have missed in the rest of what they said.
Practice noticing the shift to reply-planning the next time it happens.
lessons.apply: In your next real conversation, notice the moment your attention shifts to planning a reply, and deliberately bring it back to listening until they've finished.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you responded to only the first half of what someone said, because you'd started planning your reply too early. What did you miss?

lessons.title: Listening, Put Together
objectives: Combine attention, paraphrasing, open questions and listening-to-understand into one real conversation.
teach: This week built four pieces of real listening: full attention, confirming understanding through paraphrase, asking genuinely open questions, and catching yourself when you've switched to reply-planning instead of listening.

Doing one of these well while missing another in the same conversation — giving full attention but asking a leading question, or paraphrasing well but having already half-formulated a rebuttal underneath it.
All four point the same direction: toward actually taking in what the other person is saying, rather than performing the outward signs of listening while your own agenda runs underneath.
lessons.example: A colleague raises a concern. Giving full attention (not checking your phone), you listen all the way through without drafting a rebuttal, ask "what would help here?" rather than "don't you think it'll be fine?", and paraphrase their concern back before responding — all four together, not just one.
practicePrompts: Think of an upcoming conversation that matters.
Plan to check yourself against all four: attention, paraphrasing, open questions, listening not rebutting.
Notice afterward which one was hardest to actually do.
lessons.apply: In your next real conversation, deliberately practise all four together: full attention, a genuine paraphrase, an open question, and catching yourself if you start reply-planning early.
lessons.reflect: Across this week, which of the four — attention, paraphrasing, open questions, or listening-not-responding — is hardest for you personally?

lessons.title: Do They Want Solutions, or to Be Heard?
objectives: Tell apart a request for solutions from a desire to be heard, and respond to which one is actually being asked for.
teach: Someone describing a problem sometimes wants it solved, and sometimes just wants to be heard — venting, processing out loud, or simply wanting acknowledgment. Offering a solution to someone who wanted to vent can land as dismissive, even when the solution is good.
Assuming every problem described is a request to solve it. Jumping straight to fixes, unasked, can cut off the part of the conversation where the person actually processes what happened.
When it's unclear which is wanted, asking directly — "do you want ideas, or do you just want to vent?" — is simpler and more reliable than guessing from tone alone.
lessons.example: A friend describes a frustrating interaction with a family member, in detail, with clear emotion. Jumping straight to "here's what you should do" can land as dismissive of the actual frustration — asking "do you want my take, or do you just need to get this out?" lets them tell you which they actually want.
practicePrompts: Think of a recent time someone described a problem to you.
Consider whether they actually wanted it solved, or wanted to be heard.
Think of how you'd ask directly next time, rather than guessing.
lessons.apply: Next time someone describes a problem, ask directly whether they want ideas or just want to be heard, rather than assuming.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time someone offered you a solution when you really just wanted to vent. How did that land?

lessons.title: What's Not Being Said
objectives: Notice omissions, hesitations, and avoided topics as information, not just the content that was explicitly said.
teach: What someone doesn't mention, hesitates over, or visibly steers away from is itself information, alongside what they do say — a detailed account that skips entirely over one obvious person or moment is worth noticing.
Only tracking the content that's explicitly said, missing a conspicuous gap, hesitation, or avoided topic that's sitting right alongside it.
Noticing an omission isn't the same as knowing why it's there — it's a cue worth holding (and maybe gently asking about), not a confirmed conclusion about what's being hidden.
lessons.example: A colleague gives a detailed account of a project's problems, mentioning every team member except one, who happens to be central to the issue. The omission is worth noticing — not as proof of a specific grievance, but as something that might be worth a gentle, direct question later.
practicePrompts: Think of a recent detailed account someone gave you.
Consider what was noticeably absent from it.
Think of how you might gently ask about an omission without assuming what it means.
lessons.apply: In your next conversation, notice not just what's said but what's conspicuously left out, hesitated over, or avoided.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you later learned something important that someone had clearly avoided mentioning. Was there a cue you missed at the time?

lessons.title: Ask, Don't Assume
objectives: Ask a clarifying question when something is unclear, rather than filling the gap with an assumption.
teach: When something someone says is genuinely unclear, a direct clarifying question is almost always cheaper and more reliable than filling the gap with an assumption and acting on it.
Filling an unclear point with whatever explanation comes to mind first, then treating that filled-in version as if it were actually said.
Clarifying questions don't need to be elaborate — "what do you mean by that?" or "can you say more?" usually does the job, and signals genuine engagement rather than impatience.
lessons.example: A colleague says a deadline "might be tight." Assuming this means "probably fine" versus assuming it means "likely to slip" are both guesses — asking "tight as in we might miss it, or tight as in it'll be close but doable?" actually finds out, rather than planning around an assumption either way.
practicePrompts: Think of a recent unclear statement someone made to you.
Notice what assumption you filled the gap with.
Draft the clarifying question you could have asked instead.
lessons.apply: Next time something someone says is genuinely unclear, ask a direct clarifying question before acting on an assumption.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time an assumption you filled an unclear gap with turned out to be wrong. What would asking have avoided?

lessons.title: Listening Across a Different Style
objectives: Adjust how you listen for someone whose communication style or background genuinely differs from your own, rather than assuming your own style is the default.
teach: People genuinely differ in communication style — some are direct, some indirect; some think out loud, some process silently before speaking; norms around pace, volume, and directness vary across backgrounds and cultures too.

Listening and interpreting everyone through your own default style, without adjusting — reading someone's indirectness as evasiveness, or someone's silence as disengagement, when it's simply a different normal way of communicating.

Adjusting doesn't mean guessing at every possible cultural difference in advance — it means staying aware that your own style isn't the universal baseline, and being willing to ask or notice when someone's pattern genuinely differs from yours.
lessons.example: A team member who processes thoughts silently before speaking takes longer pauses in discussions than a colleague who thinks out loud. Reading the pause as disengagement or lack of a view, rather than simply a different processing style, risks cutting off a real contribution before it's had time to form.
practicePrompts: Think of someone whose communication style genuinely differs from your own.
Consider a time you may have misread their style through your own default lens.
Think of what adjusting your listening for them might actually look like.
lessons.apply: With someone whose communication style differs from yours, consciously adjust your listening — more patience for pauses, more directness in checking understanding — rather than defaulting to your own norm.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time your own communication style was misread by someone who assumed their style was the default. What would you have wanted them to understand instead?

lessons.title: Responding Well
objectives: Combine venting-vs-solving, listening for the unsaid, clarifying over assuming, and listening across difference into one complete response to a real conversation.
Describe a real conversation, using everything covered across both listening modules.
teach: This week covered telling venting from problem-solving, noticing what's unsaid, asking instead of assuming, and adjusting for a different communication style. Together with last week's attention, paraphrasing, open questions and listening-not-responding, that's eight habits for genuinely hearing someone.

Treating good listening as a performance — the right nods, the right pauses — rather than the actual, quieter discipline all eight of these ideas point toward: attending fully, confirming understanding, noticing gaps, asking rather than guessing, and adjusting for real differences in how people communicate.
This closes out both listening modules. The next module, on feedback, assumes this kind of listening as its foundation — feedback given or received without it tends to go badly.
lessons.example: A friend from a different cultural background describes a work conflict indirectly, with noticeable pauses and no direct mention of one colleague. Reading this well means adjusting for their style (not misreading indirectness as evasiveness), noticing the omission without assuming its meaning, asking a clarifying question about what they actually want from the conversation (venting or advice), rather than guessing from tone alone.
practicePrompts: Think of a real, upcoming or recent conversation.
Check it against all eight ideas from this week and last.
Consider what you'd do differently with all eight in mind.
lessons.apply: In your next real conversation that matters, deliberately bring all eight listening ideas to it, not just the ones that come naturally.
lessons.reflect: In your own words, describe a real recent conversation, and check it against as many of these eight listening ideas as actually apply.

lessons.title: Say What Actually Happened
objectives: Describe feedback as a specific, observed behavior rather than a vague trait or judgment.
teach: Useful feedback describes a specific, observed behavior — what was said or done, and when — rather than a vague trait ("you're disorganized") that the person can't actually act on.

Giving feedback as a general trait or character judgment rather than a specific instance. "You're not a team player" gives no actionable handle; "you didn't loop the team in on the schedule change" does.
The test is whether the feedback points to a specific moment the person can actually remember and address, not a sweeping characterization they're left to guess at.
lessons.example: "You're careless with details" is a trait judgment with no clear next step. "The report you sent Tuesday had three numbers that didn't match the spreadsheet" names a specific, checkable instance the person can actually do something about.
practicePrompts: Think of vague feedback you've given or received.
Identify what specific instance it was probably pointing at.
Rewrite it as a specific, observed behavior.
lessons.apply: Next time you give feedback, replace any trait language with a specific, dated instance of what was actually said or done.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you received vague feedback and weren't sure what to actually do differently. What specific instance might it have been about?

lessons.title: Critique the Action, Not the Person
objectives: Give feedback that addresses a specific action, without labeling the person's character.
teach: Feedback aimed at an action ("this missed the deadline") is easier to hear and act on than feedback that labels the person ("you're unreliable") — even when both are responding to the same event.

Reaching for a character label when the actual target is one action. It's a short step from "this was late" to "you're always late," but the second is a judgment of identity, not a description of an event.
Separating the two doesn't mean softening the message — a specific, direct critique of an action can be just as honest as a character label, without the same defensive reaction it tends to provoke.
lessons.example: "You're unreliable" labels the person. "This is the second deadline this month that's slipped without a heads-up" names a specific pattern of actions — direct, but aimed at behavior, not identity.
practicePrompts: Think of feedback you've given that labeled a person's character.
Identify the specific action underneath the label.
Rewrite the feedback aimed at the action instead.
lessons.apply: Next time you're about to say "you're [trait]", stop and name the specific action instead.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time feedback about one action got generalized into a judgment about who you are. How did that land, compared to feedback about just the action?

lessons.title: Choosing When and How
objectives: Choose a time and framing for feedback that lets it actually be heard, rather than ambushing the person.
teach: The same feedback lands differently depending on when and how it's delivered — privately versus in front of others, right after an incident versus much later, with warning versus out of nowhere.

Delivering feedback as an ambush — publicly, with no warning, or at a moment when the person can't actually process or respond to it. Even accurate feedback can fail here simply because of how it arrived.

Good timing and framing isn't about softening the content — it's about choosing a moment and setting where the person is actually in a position to hear it, rather than just defend against the delivery.
lessons.example: Correcting someone's error in front of the whole team, mid-meeting, tends to trigger a defensive reaction regardless of how fair the correction is. The same point, raised privately afterward, is far more likely to actually land.
practicePrompts: Think of feedback you've received that was well-timed or poorly-timed.
Identify what made the timing or setting work or not work.
Consider how you'd choose timing for feedback you need to give soon.
lessons.apply: Before your next piece of corrective feedback, deliberately choose a private, well-timed moment rather than the first available one.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time feedback was delivered as an ambush — in public, or with no warning. How did the setting itself affect how it was received?

lessons.title: An Accurate Picture, Not Just Criticism
objectives: Give feedback that balances honest corrective content with acknowledgment of what's working.
teach: Useful feedback gives an accurate picture — what's working, alongside what isn't — rather than only corrective content, which can make a genuinely strong performance look uniformly bad.
Overloading feedback with only criticism (demoralizing, and an inaccurate picture if other things are going well), or the opposite: only praise, with real problems left unsaid to avoid discomfort.
Balance isn't a fixed ratio of positive-to-negative comments — it's giving feedback that's actually accurate to the full situation, not padded or softened for its own sake.
lessons.example: A review that lists five things that went wrong and nothing that went right leaves someone with a distorted picture if, in fact, most of the work was solid. A review that's all praise, omitting a real recurring problem, is just as inaccurate in the other direction.
practicePrompts: Think of feedback you've given that was all criticism or all praise.
Consider what got left out of the picture either way.
Think of how you'd give a more accurate, balanced version.
lessons.apply: In your next piece of feedback, deliberately check that it reflects the full accurate picture — not padded with empty praise, not stripped of what's actually working.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you received feedback that was only criticism or only praise. What would a more accurate, balanced version have included?

lessons.title: Giving Feedback, Put Together
objectives: Combine specificity, separating behavior from character, timing, and balance into one piece of real feedback.
teach: This week built four pieces of giving feedback well: being specific instead of vague, aiming at the action instead of the person, choosing timing and framing that can actually be heard, and keeping the picture balanced and accurate.

Doing one of these well while missing another — being specific but delivering it as a public ambush, or balanced but still vague enough that neither the praise nor the correction points to anything concrete.
All four point the same direction: feedback that's actually useful to the person receiving it, not just accurate from the giver's point of view.
lessons.example: Pulling a colleague aside privately (timing), to note that "the client email on Tuesday missed the pricing update" (specific, aimed at the action, not "you're careless"), alongside acknowledging that the rest of the proposal was strong (balance) — all four together, not just one.
practicePrompts: Think of feedback you need to give soon.
Draft it checking all four: specific, aimed at the action, well-timed, balanced.
Notice which of the four was hardest to actually include.
lessons.apply: The next time you give real feedback, deliberately check it against all four ideas before delivering it.
lessons.reflect: Across this week, which of the four — specificity, separating action from character, timing, or balance — is hardest for you personally to get right?

lessons.title: Taking It In Before Responding
objectives: Take in feedback before responding, rather than justifying or explaining it away immediately.
teach: Feedback, especially corrective feedback, triggers an instinct to justify or explain immediately. Taking it in first — before responding at all — gives you a chance to actually process what's being said.
Jumping straight to a defense or explanation before the feedback has been fully taken in. This can look like listening from the outside, while the content is barely registering underneath.
Taking a moment — even just a breath, or saying "let me think about that" — before responding isn't the same as agreeing with everything said. It just separates understanding from reacting.
lessons.example: A manager points out a missed step in a process. The instinct is to immediately explain why it happened. Pausing first — "let me make sure I understand what you're pointing to" — actually confirms what's being said before responding to it, defensively or otherwise.
practicePrompts: Think of a recent time you received feedback and responded defensively right away.
Consider what you might have missed by responding before fully taking it in.
Practice pausing before responding, the next time feedback comes.
lessons.apply: Next time you receive feedback, pause before responding — even briefly — rather than justifying immediately.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you reacted defensively to feedback before you'd actually taken it in. What might you have understood differently with a pause first?

lessons.title: It's About One Thing You Did, Not Who You Are
objectives: Treat critical feedback as information about a specific action, not a judgment of one's fundamental worth.
teach: Critical feedback about a specific action is information about that instance, not a verdict on someone's fundamental worth or identity — even when it stings in a way that feels personal.
Expanding a specific critique into a global judgment about yourself — "I made an error in this report" becoming "I'm bad at this job" or "I'm not good enough."
Keeping the two separate doesn't mean feedback never feels uncomfortable — it means not letting one specific critique expand into a conclusion about your overall worth or competence.
lessons.example: A piece of feedback that a presentation ran too long and lost the room is information about that one presentation. Hearing it as "I'm bad at public speaking" or "I'm not cut out for this" expands one specific instance into a much larger, harder-to-shake judgment that the feedback never actually made.
practicePrompts: Think of a time critical feedback felt like a judgment on your overall worth.
Identify the specific, narrower thing the feedback was actually about.
Notice the gap between the specific feedback and the broader judgment you added.
lessons.apply: Next time feedback stings, check whether you're reacting to the specific point made or to a broader judgment you've added on top of it.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you let one piece of critical feedback expand into a judgment about your overall worth or ability. What was the feedback actually, specifically about?

lessons.title: Asking What That Actually Means
objectives: Ask for specifics when feedback is vague, rather than accepting it without clarification.
teach: Vague feedback ("this needs more polish," "be more proactive") is hard to act on as given. Asking directly what it specifically refers to turns it into something usable.
Accepting vague feedback at face value, nodding along without actually knowing what to change, then guessing at what might have been meant.
Asking for specifics isn't pushing back on the feedback — it's the step that makes vague feedback genuinely useful, by turning a general impression into something concrete enough to act on.
lessons.example: "This presentation needs more polish" doesn't say what to actually change. Asking "can you point to a specific slide or section where that was most noticeable?" turns a vague impression into something that can actually be fixed.
practicePrompts: Think of vague feedback you've received and accepted without clarifying.
Draft the clarifying question you could have asked.
Consider what concrete change the clarified version might have pointed to.
lessons.apply: Next time you receive vague feedback, ask directly for a specific example before trying to act on it.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you acted on vague feedback by guessing what it meant, rather than asking. Did your guess match what was actually meant?

lessons.title: Not All Feedback Is Equally Worth Acting On
objectives: Judge which feedback is actually worth acting on, rather than treating every piece of feedback as equally valid.
teach: Feedback varies in how much weight it deserves — a pattern repeated by several people carries more than a single offhand comment; feedback from someone with direct relevant expertise carries more than a passing opinion.
Treating every piece of feedback received as equally valid and actionable, regardless of who it's from, how often it's been said, or whether it fits the actual context.

Weighing feedback isn't dismissing anything uncomfortable — it's judging, honestly, which specific pieces are actually worth acting on, based on the source and the pattern, not just reacting to whichever one landed most recently.
lessons.example: One client's offhand comment about a proposal's formatting is worth noting but not necessarily acting on. The same formatting concern, raised independently by three different clients over two months, is a real pattern worth taking seriously.
practicePrompts: Think of a piece of feedback you acted on without weighing its source or how often it had come up.
Think of a piece of feedback you dismissed that, in hindsight, deserved more weight.
Consider how you'd weigh a piece of feedback you've recently received.
lessons.apply: The next time you receive feedback, weigh it by source and pattern before deciding how much to act on it.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you treated a single piece of feedback as more decisive than it deserved, or a repeated pattern as less decisive than it deserved. What would weighing it more carefully have changed?

lessons.title: Receiving Feedback Well, Put Together
objectives: Combine receiving without defensiveness, separating feedback from self-worth, asking for specifics, and weighing feedback selectively into one complete response.
Describe a real piece of feedback you've received, using everything covered across both feedback modules.
teach: This week covered receiving feedback without immediate defensiveness, keeping it separate from self-worth, asking for specifics when it's vague, and weighing which feedback is actually worth acting on. Together with last week's giving-feedback habits, that's eight ideas for feedback working well in both directions.

Treating feedback as something to survive rather than genuinely use — either shutting down defensively, or accepting everything uncritically without weighing it, both of which skip the actual work of taking feedback in and judging it honestly.

This closes out both feedback modules. The next module, on perspective-taking, builds on this: understanding someone else's view requires some of the same discipline — taking it in before reacting — that receiving feedback well requires.
lessons.example: A colleague gives you blunt, vague feedback ("this isn't working") in front of others. Receiving it well means pausing rather than justifying immediately, not reading it as a verdict on your competence, asking afterward what specifically wasn't working, and then honestly weighing how much to actually change based on whether this is a one-off comment or a pattern others have also raised.
practicePrompts: Think of a real piece of feedback you've recently received.
Check it against all eight ideas from this week and last.
Consider what you'd do differently with all eight in mind.
lessons.apply: The next time you receive real feedback that matters, deliberately bring all eight feedback ideas to it, not just the ones that come naturally.
lessons.reflect: In your own words, describe a real piece of feedback you've received, and check it against as many of these eight feedback ideas as actually apply.

lessons.title: Their View, Not Yours, Reflected Back
objectives: Imagine someone's actual, possibly different view of a situation, rather than assuming they see it the way you do.
teach: Perspective-taking means actually imagining someone else's distinct view of a situation — their information, priorities, and history with it — not assuming they see it the way you do.

Projection: quietly substituting your own view for theirs, and treating that substitution as if it were genuine perspective-taking. It often doesn't feel like an assumption — it feels like obvious common sense.

The test is whether you can describe their view in terms that could turn out to be wrong — if your account of their perspective is indistinguishable from your own opinion, it's probably projection, not perspective-taking.
lessons.example: Assuming a colleague who missed a deadline must not care about the project, because that's how you'd feel if you missed one, skips over the possibility that they're dealing with something you don't know about — a different possibility than the one your own view supplies by default.
practicePrompts: Think of a time you assumed someone saw a situation the way you did.
Consider what their actual, possibly different view might have been.
Notice whether your assumption could have turned out wrong.
lessons.apply: Before assuming how someone sees a situation, ask yourself whether your account of their view could turn out to be wrong — if not, you may be projecting rather than imagining their actual view.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time someone assumed your view matched theirs, when it didn't. What did they miss by not actually imagining your perspective?

lessons.title: What They Know That You Don't
objectives: Account for what the other person does or doesn't know, rather than judging their reaction as if they shared your full information.
teach: People act and react based on what they actually know, which often isn't the same as what you know — you might have context they lack, or they might have context you lack.
Judging someone's reaction as if they had your full information, without checking whether a knowledge gap — in either direction — explains the difference.

Resolving a knowledge asymmetry usually just means asking what the other person actually knows, rather than assuming either that they know what you know, or that you know everything relevant to their reaction.
lessons.example: A teammate seems unreasonably frustrated by a schedule change that seems minor to you — until you learn they'd already told a client a date based on the old schedule, information you didn't have. Their reaction made sense once the knowledge gap was accounted for.
practicePrompts: Think of a time someone's reaction seemed disproportionate until you learned what they knew that you didn't.
Think of a time you reacted strongly to something because of information others didn't have.
Consider how checking for a knowledge gap might change your read of a recent disagreement.
lessons.apply: Next time someone's reaction seems disproportionate, ask what they might know that you don't, before concluding their reaction is unreasonable.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time your own reaction to something seemed confusing to someone else because they didn't know something you did. What would explaining that gap have clarified?

lessons.title: How It Probably Feels, Not Just What They Think
objectives: Infer how a situation likely feels to someone, not just what they think about it.
teach: Perspective-taking includes the emotional dimension — how a situation likely feels to someone — not just the cognitive one, what they probably think or believe about it.
Working out someone's view purely as an information problem (what do they know, what do they conclude) while skipping over how the situation likely feels to them.

Emotional perspective-taking doesn't require guessing a precise emotion — it means at minimum registering that a situation likely carries some emotional weight for the other person, not just a factual position.
lessons.example: Understanding that a colleague disagrees with a reorg decision on the merits (the cognitive view) is only part of the picture if the reorg also means losing a team they built over years — the loss likely carries real emotional weight that a purely factual read of their position would miss.
practicePrompts: Think of a disagreement where you understood someone's reasoning but not how the situation felt to them.
Consider what emotional weight the situation might have carried for them.
Notice the difference between understanding their position and understanding their experience of it.
lessons.apply: In your next disagreement with someone, consciously ask not just what they think, but how the situation likely feels to them.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time someone understood your reasoning but missed how the situation actually felt to you. What was missing from their understanding?

lessons.title: Checking Your Read of Someone Else
objectives: Check an inferred read of someone's perspective against what they actually say, rather than treating the inference as confirmed.
teach: An inferred read of someone's perspective is a guess, however informed — checking it against what they actually say ("is that right, or am I missing something?") is what turns a guess into something confirmed.
Treating an empathic read as established fact, acting on it confidently without ever checking whether it matches what the person would actually say about their own view.
Checking doesn't undermine the empathic effort — it's the step that makes it reliable, the same way paraphrasing confirms understanding rather than replacing it.
lessons.example: Inferring that a quiet teammate is upset about being passed over for a project, and then checking directly ("you've seemed a bit off since the project announcement — is that what's going on, or is it something else?") rather than acting on the guess as if it were confirmed.
practicePrompts: Think of a time you acted on an inferred read of someone's feelings without checking it.
Consider whether the read turned out to be accurate.
Draft how you'd check a current read of someone's perspective directly.
lessons.apply: Next time you form a read of someone's perspective or feelings, check it directly with them rather than acting on the guess alone.
