lessons.reflect: Think of a time someone's inferred read of your perspective turned out to be wrong, because they never checked it with you. What would checking have caught?

lessons.title: Seeing It From Where They Stand, Put Together
objectives: Combine avoiding projection, accounting for knowledge gaps, emotional perspective-taking, and checking your read into one complete approach to understanding someone else's view.
teach: This week built four pieces of actually seeing a situation from someone else's standpoint: avoiding projection, accounting for what they know that you don't (or vice versa), considering how it likely feels and not just what they think, and checking your read rather than assuming it's accurate.
Doing one well while skipping another — genuinely imagining their distinct view but never checking whether the guess is right, or checking a read that was projection all along.
All four point the same direction: an accurate understanding of someone else's actual standpoint, built and then verified, not assumed from your own.
lessons.example: A colleague seems unusually upset about a decision. Rather than assuming they feel the way you would (avoiding projection), you consider what they might know that you don't (a prior commitment affected by the decision), register that this likely carries real emotional weight for them (not just a disagreement on the merits), and then check directly: "this seems to have hit you harder than I expected — is that about the decision itself, or something else going on?"
practicePrompts: Think of someone whose current perspective you're unsure about.
Walk through all four: avoid projecting, consider knowledge gaps, consider the emotional weight, then check directly.
Notice which of the four was hardest to actually do.
lessons.apply: The next time you're trying to understand someone else's view, deliberately walk through all four ideas before concluding you understand it.
lessons.reflect: Across this week, which of the four — avoiding projection, knowledge gaps, emotional perspective-taking, or checking your read — is hardest for you personally?

lessons.title: Understandable Doesn't Mean You Agree
objectives: Acknowledge someone's perspective as understandable without necessarily agreeing with their conclusion or decision.
teach: Acknowledging that someone's perspective makes sense, given what they know and feel, is a separate act from agreeing with their conclusion or decision — you can genuinely validate the first without conceding the second.

Believing that saying "I understand why you feel that way" commits you to agreeing with the resulting decision, which leads to either withholding validation to avoid that commitment, or offering validation as a disguised concession.
A clean validation names the specific thing that's understandable ("given what happened, I get why you're frustrated") without implying the conclusion that follows from it is one you share.
lessons.example: "I get why you'd want to walk away from this deal, given how the last round went" validates the frustration driving the position, without committing to agreeing that walking away is actually the right call — those are two separate claims.
practicePrompts: Think of a time you withheld validating someone because you didn't want to seem to agree with their conclusion.
Consider how you could have validated the feeling without conceding the conclusion.
Draft a validation that names the understandable part specifically, separate from the decision.
lessons.apply: Next time you disagree with someone's conclusion, practice validating the understandable part of their perspective explicitly, without implying you agree with where they land.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time someone validated your perspective without agreeing with your conclusion. How did that distinction come across, and did it still feel genuine?

lessons.title: Knowing Your Own Limit
objectives: Recognize and set a reasonable limit on empathic engagement, rather than overextending indefinitely.
teach: Empathic engagement has a real cost, and a sustainable limit — recognizing that limit, and setting a boundary around it, is part of being able to engage well rather than a failure of empathy.

Continuing to extend full empathic engagement well past a sustainable point, without noticing the cost or setting any limit, which tends to produce either burnout or a quieter withdrawal from engaging at all.
Setting a limit doesn't mean caring less — it means engaging in a way that can actually be sustained, rather than running the capacity for empathy down to nothing.
lessons.example: Someone who always makes themselves available to listen to a friend's repeated, unchanging crisis, at real cost to their own time and energy, may eventually have nothing left to offer — recognizing a limit ("I can talk for twenty minutes, but I need to go after that") keeps the engagement sustainable instead of running it to zero.
practicePrompts: Think of a time you extended empathic engagement well past what was sustainable for you.
Consider what a reasonable limit would have looked like.
Think of a current relationship where setting a limit might help you keep engaging well, rather than withdrawing entirely.
lessons.apply: Identify one relationship where you tend to overextend empathically, and set one concrete, reasonable limit this week.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you didn't set a limit on empathic engagement and later felt depleted or resentful. What limit, in hindsight, would have kept you able to keep engaging?

lessons.title: Still Trying to Understand, Even in Disagreement
objectives: Maintain genuine perspective-taking even during a heated disagreement, rather than abandoning it.
teach: Perspective-taking is hardest, and most valuable, exactly when a disagreement is heated — genuinely understanding the other side's view doesn't require giving up your own position.
Dropping any attempt to understand the other person's view as soon as a disagreement escalates, as if perspective-taking and holding a firm position were incompatible.

Maintaining perspective-taking in conflict means being able to state the other side's view accurately, in terms they'd recognize as fair, while still disagreeing with it — not conceding, just understanding.
lessons.example: In a heated disagreement about a project decision, being able to say "I think you're worried this delays the launch past a commitment you've already made — is that the core of it?" while still holding your own position is a sign perspective-taking hasn't been abandoned, even though the disagreement is real.
practicePrompts: Think of a heated disagreement where you stopped trying to understand the other side's view.
Consider what their view actually was, as they would have described it.
Practice stating the other side's view fairly, in a recent or ongoing disagreement, without conceding your own position.
lessons.apply: In your next heated disagreement, try to state the other person's view in terms they'd recognize as fair, before continuing to argue your own.
lessons.reflect: Think of a disagreement where someone kept trying to understand your view even while disagreeing with you. How did that affect the disagreement itself?

lessons.title: Honest and Caring, Not One or the Other
objectives: Combine directness with care, rather than treating honesty and compassion as a tradeoff.
teach: Honesty and care aren't a tradeoff — a direct, truthful message delivered with real care for how it lands is both more honest and more useful than either a softened version or a blunt one.
Treating directness and care as mutually exclusive — believing honesty requires bluntness regardless of impact, or that care requires softening or withholding the truth.
Compassionate directness means saying the true thing clearly, while genuinely attending to the other person's experience of hearing it — neither sacrificed for the other.
lessons.example: "This isn't working and I don't think it's going to get better" said with care for the moment and the person, rather than either softened into vague hints that obscure the actual message, or delivered bluntly with no attention to how it lands — the same honest content, delivered with genuine care.
practicePrompts: Think of a time you softened a true message to the point it didn't land clearly.
Think of a time you delivered a true message bluntly, without attending to how it landed.
Draft a version of a message you need to deliver that's both direct and genuinely caring.
lessons.apply: The next time you need to deliver a hard truth, draft it so it's fully honest and attends to how it will land for the other person — not one at the expense of the other.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time someone delivered hard feedback or news to you in a way that was both honest and genuinely caring. What made it land as both?

lessons.title: Responding to Someone Else's View, Put Together
objectives: Combine validating without agreeing, recognizing empathic limits, maintaining perspective-taking under disagreement, and compassionate directness into one complete response to someone else's view.
Describe a real situation involving someone else's perspective, using everything covered across both perspective-taking modules.
teach: This week covered validating a perspective without agreeing with it, recognizing a sustainable limit on empathic engagement, maintaining perspective-taking even in disagreement, and combining honesty with care. Together with last week's perspective-taking habits, that's eight ideas for understanding and responding to someone else's view well.
Treating empathy as either unconditional agreement or an unlimited resource, both of which break down — unconditional agreement collapses your own position, and an unlimited resource runs out.

This closes out both perspective-taking modules, and with them, the ten-module arc covering observation, pattern-reading, signals, listening, feedback, and perspective-taking — different facets of reading situations and people well.
lessons.example: A friend is upset about a decision you disagree with. Responding well means validating the frustration as understandable (without agreeing the decision was wrong), maintaining a genuine attempt to see their view even while disagreeing, recognizing your own limit if the conversation runs long, and being honest about your actual disagreement with real care for how it lands — all four together.
practicePrompts: Think of a real, current or recent situation involving someone else's perspective.
Check it against all eight ideas from this week and last.
Consider what you'd do differently with all eight in mind.
lessons.apply: In your next conversation involving a genuinely different perspective, deliberately bring all eight ideas to it, not just the ones that come naturally.
lessons.reflect: In your own words, describe a real situation involving someone else's perspective, and check it against as many of these eight ideas as actually apply.

lessons.title: What Actually Earns Trust Over Time
objectives: Recognize that trust is built through predictable follow-through over time, not single impressive gestures.
teach: Trust is built mainly through a predictable pattern of follow-through over time — doing what you said you'd do, repeatedly — not through any single impressive or generous gesture, however memorable.

Treating one striking act of generosity or competence as strong evidence of overall trustworthiness, while the slower, less visible pattern of whether someone reliably follows through gets comparatively little weight.

A single gesture can be genuine and still tell you little about whether someone is consistent — consistency is demonstrated by a pattern across many smaller, less memorable moments, not by any one of them.
lessons.example: A new colleague makes a generous, visible gesture early on — covering for someone during a crunch — which feels like strong evidence of trustworthiness. Whether they reliably follow through on smaller, routine commitments over the following months is actually the better evidence, even though it's far less memorable than the one gesture.
practicePrompts: Think of someone whose trustworthiness you judged mainly from one memorable gesture.
Consider what their actual pattern of smaller follow-through has been since.
Notice the gap, if any, between the memorable gesture and the ongoing pattern.
lessons.apply: This week, notice at least one case where you're judging someone's trustworthiness from a single gesture, and deliberately look instead at their pattern of smaller follow-through.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time a single impressive gesture led you to trust someone more than their actual ongoing pattern later supported. What did the pattern eventually reveal?

lessons.title: Sharing at the Right Pace
objectives: Match self-disclosure to a relationship's actual pace and reciprocity, rather than oversharing or undersharing.
teach: Rapport builds through self-disclosure that's roughly reciprocal and matched to how close the relationship actually is — sharing a bit more as the relationship develops, not all at once and not never.

Sharing personal information far ahead of the relationship's actual closeness (which can feel overwhelming or presumptuous), or far behind it (which can feel withholding and slow any real connection), rather than roughly matching the other person's pace.

Calibration isn't a fixed formula — it means noticing and roughly matching the pace the other person is actually setting, rather than defaulting to your own habitual level of disclosure regardless of context.
lessons.example: Sharing a significant personal struggle in detail with someone met an hour ago, before any real reciprocal closeness has developed, tends to land as overwhelming rather than connecting — the same disclosure, offered later as the relationship develops and the other person has shared comparably, tends to build real rapport instead.
practicePrompts: Think of a time disclosure felt mismatched to a relationship's actual pace, in either direction.
Consider what a better-matched pace would have looked like.
Notice the pace of disclosure in a current relationship you're building.
lessons.apply: In a relationship you're currently building, notice the other person's pace of disclosure this week, and try to roughly match it rather than defaulting to your own habitual level.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time someone's disclosure to you felt mismatched to the relationship's actual closeness — too much, too soon, or too little, too late. How did it affect the relationship?

lessons.title: Trusting Based on Track Record, Not Charm
objectives: Extend trust based on someone's demonstrated track record, rather than their likability or charisma alone.
teach: How much trust to extend to someone should track their actual, demonstrated history of following through — not how likable, charming, or confident they come across, which is a separate quality entirely.
Extending a significant degree of trust based mainly on likability or charisma, which can be entirely genuine and still tell you little about whether someone reliably follows through on commitments.

This isn't cynicism about likable people — it's simply keeping two separate questions separate: do I enjoy this person's company, and has this person actually demonstrated reliability, which don't have to have the same answer.
lessons.example: A charismatic new business partner who is genuinely enjoyable to work with hasn't yet demonstrated any actual track record of following through on commitments — extending the same level of trust given to someone with years of demonstrated reliability, based on charisma alone, conflates two separate questions.
practicePrompts: Think of someone you trusted quickly mainly because you liked them.
Consider what their actual track record was at the time, separate from how likable they were.
Notice the two questions — likability and demonstrated reliability — in a current relationship.
lessons.apply: Before extending a significant degree of trust to someone new, separately ask how likable they are and what their actual demonstrated track record is, rather than letting the first answer stand in for the second.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you extended trust based on likability that the person's actual track record didn't yet support. What happened?

lessons.title: Rebuilding Trust After It Breaks
objectives: Rebuild broken trust through sustained, consistent follow-through, rather than relying on an apology alone.
teach: Rebuilding trust after a breach requires a sustained pattern of consistent follow-through over time — the same thing that built trust in the first place — not a single apology, however sincere.

Treating a verbal apology as sufficient on its own to repair broken trust, expecting the relationship to reset immediately once the words have been said, without the following period of demonstrated reliability.
A genuine apology is usually a necessary first step, but it's the start of the repair process, not the whole of it — the trust is actually rebuilt by what happens afterward, consistently, over time.
lessons.example: After missing an important commitment, a sincere apology is offered — but trust is actually rebuilt afterward, by following through reliably on the next several smaller commitments, not by the apology itself, however genuine it was in the moment.
practicePrompts: Think of a time an apology alone was expected to repair broken trust, and whether it actually did.
Consider what sustained follow-through, rather than just the apology, would have required.
Think of a relationship where trust is currently being rebuilt, and what a consistent pattern going forward would look like.
lessons.apply: If you're currently rebuilding trust with someone after a breach, identify one small, concrete commitment you can follow through on consistently, rather than relying on the apology alone.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you had to rebuild someone's trust in you after breaking it. What actually rebuilt it — the apology, or what you did afterward?

lessons.title: Earning and Extending Trust, Put Together
objectives: Combine consistency, calibrated disclosure, trust-by-track-record, and trust repair into one complete approach to building and maintaining trust.
teach: This week built four pieces of earning and extending trust well: recognizing that consistency, not single gestures, builds trust; matching self-disclosure to a relationship's actual pace; calibrating trust to someone's actual track record rather than their charm; and rebuilding trust after a breach through sustained follow-through, not just an apology.
Doing one well while missing another — extending trust based on a likable person's one impressive gesture, or rebuilding a breach with an apology but no actual change in behavior afterward.
All four point the same direction: trust tracks a real, demonstrated pattern over time, in both directions — earning it and repairing it — not any single moment, gesture, or word.
lessons.example: A new working relationship develops well: disclosure is paced to match growing closeness (not rushed), trust is extended gradually as a track record of follow-through accumulates (not based on charm alone), and when one commitment is missed, trust is rebuilt afterward through a sustained pattern of reliability, not just an apology — consistency running through all of it.
practicePrompts: Think of a relationship where trust is currently developing or being repaired.
Check it against all four: consistency, calibrated disclosure, track record, repair.
Notice which of the four is hardest for you personally to actually apply.
lessons.apply: In a relationship you're currently building or repairing, deliberately apply whichever of these four ideas is most relevant this week.
lessons.reflect: Across this week, which of the four — consistency, calibrated disclosure, trust-by-track-record, or repair — is hardest for you personally to get right?

lessons.title: A Conversation That Tests Everything
objectives: Combine observation vs. interpretation, active listening, and checking an empathic read in one real, complex conversation.
teach: A single real conversation can call on everything this course has covered: separating what was actually observed from the story added about it, giving genuine attention rather than half-listening, and checking an inferred read of someone's feelings rather than acting on the guess alone.

Doing one of these well in isolation — listening attentively, say — while skipping another, like treating an interpretation as if it were the observed fact, or acting on an empathic guess without ever checking it.
This course has built these as separate skills, module by module, but a real conversation doesn't separate them — they all operate at once, and missing any one of them can undo the others.
lessons.example: A friend goes quiet mid-conversation. The observed fact is the silence itself; the interpretation ("they're annoyed with me") is a separate, unconfirmed story. Giving full attention rather than filling the silence with your own assumption, and then checking directly ("you went quiet there — everything okay, or is it something else?") keeps the observation, the attention, and the check all working together.
practicePrompts: Think of a real, complex conversation you've had recently.
Identify a moment where observation, attention, or checking a read was especially important.
Notice whether all three were actually present, or whether one was missing.
lessons.apply: In your next conversation that matters, deliberately notice all three: what you're actually observing versus interpreting, whether you're giving full attention, and whether you check any empathic read before acting on it.
lessons.reflect: Think of a real conversation where missing one of these three — clear observation, full attention, or checking a read — changed how it went. What would including it have changed?

lessons.title: Feedback From Someone You're Reading Wrong
objectives: Combine giving specific feedback, avoiding projection about someone else's view, and receiving feedback without defensiveness in one real exchange.
teach: Feedback exchanges often go wrong not because the feedback itself was poorly given, but because of an assumption about the other person's view layered on top of it — on either side of the exchange.

Assuming you know why someone gave the feedback they did, or why they're reacting the way they are to it, rather than imagining their actual, possibly different view — which can derail a perfectly specific, well-intentioned piece of feedback.

Specific feedback, an accurate read of the other person's actual perspective (not a projected one), and a non-defensive reception of it are three separate requirements — an exchange can get any one of them right while still failing on the others.
lessons.example: A manager gives specific, well-aimed feedback about a missed detail. The employee assumes the manager is trying to push them out (projection, not their manager's actual view), and responds defensively, justifying before fully hearing it. The feedback itself was fine — the exchange broke down on the other two pieces.
practicePrompts: Think of a feedback exchange that went worse than the content of the feedback itself warranted.
Identify whether a projected assumption, a defensive reaction, or both were involved.
Consider what addressing that specific piece would have changed.
lessons.apply: In your next feedback exchange, in either direction, check specifically for projection about the other person's view and for your own defensive reaction, not just the content of the feedback itself.
lessons.reflect: Think of a feedback exchange where an assumption about the other person's view, rather than the feedback's content, was the actual source of the breakdown. What was the assumption, and what was the person's actual view?

lessons.title: When the Pattern and the Trust Don't Match
objectives: Combine base-rate reasoning, checking an inferred read, and calibrating trust to someone's actual track record in one judgment about a person over time.
teach: Judging a person over time — not just a single moment — means combining how common a given behavior actually is in general (the base rate), whether an inferred read of their current state has actually been checked, and whether the trust extended to them matches their real track record, not just a recent impression.
Letting a vivid recent impression override all three — treating an unusual instance as the new baseline, skipping the check, and adjusting trust based on the moment rather than the pattern.

These three ideas reinforce each other precisely because they all push against the same error: treating one data point — a single instance, an unchecked guess, a single gesture — as more decisive than it actually is.
lessons.example: A normally reliable colleague misses one deadline. Judging them fairly means asking how common a single slip actually is for someone with their track record (base rate), checking directly rather than assuming they've become unreliable (checking the read), and weighing the one miss against their actual sustained pattern rather than letting it override the trust that pattern has earned (track record).
practicePrompts: Think of a time a single recent instance threatened to override your overall judgment of someone.
Consider what their actual base rate and track record looked like, apart from that one instance.
Notice whether you checked your read of the instance, or just acted on the impression.
lessons.apply: Next time a single recent instance makes you reconsider your trust in someone, explicitly weigh it against their base rate and track record, and check your read before acting on it.
lessons.reflect: Think of a time you let one recent instance override an otherwise solid track record, without checking whether the instance was actually representative. What did you miss by not checking?

lessons.title: The Full Picture
objectives: Combine observation, listening, feedback, perspective-taking, pattern-reading, and trust into one complete, integrated approach to reading and responding to people well.
Describe a real situation using the full range of ideas covered across the course.
teach: This course covered observation and inference, reading patterns over time, reading signals and the room, listening, giving and receiving feedback, taking someone else's perspective, and building and repairing trust — eleven modules, one underlying skill: reading a real situation and the people in it accurately, and responding well once you have.

Treating any one of these as sufficient on its own — sharp observation without real listening, genuine empathy without a checked read, specific feedback without accounting for the other person's actual perspective, a well-calibrated read of a pattern without the trust history to act on it wisely.

There's no higher module after this one — the actual test is whether these show up together, unprompted, in the ordinary situations of daily life: a hard conversation, a piece of feedback, a disagreement, a relationship that needs rebuilding.
lessons.example: A long-standing colleague seems unusually withdrawn in a meeting. Reading it well draws on nearly everything: noting the withdrawal as an observation, not yet an interpretation; listening fully rather than filling the silence with your own story; checking your read directly rather than acting on an assumption; weighing this one instance against their actual track record rather than over-reacting to it; and, if feedback or a hard conversation follows, giving it specifically and with genuine attention to their actual, not assumed, perspective.
practicePrompts: Think of a real, complex situation involving another person, recent or ongoing.
Walk through as many of this course's ideas as actually apply to it.
Notice which ideas came naturally, and which took deliberate effort.
lessons.apply: In your next genuinely complex situation involving another person, deliberately draw on as much of this course as is relevant, rather than defaulting to the one or two habits that come easiest.
lessons.reflect: Looking back across this entire course, which single idea — from observation, patterns, signals, listening, feedback, perspective-taking, or trust — has changed how you actually interact with people the most? Which one still needs the most deliberate practice?

misconceptions.label: Premature motive attribution
misconceptions.description: Assigning a specific motive to a behaviour before there is evidence that distinguishes it from other plausible motives.

misconceptions.label: Confusing observation with interpretation
misconceptions.description: Treating an inferred mental state or trait as if it were itself something directly observed.

misconceptions.label: Overgeneralising from one incident
misconceptions.description: Drawing a general conclusion about a person's character from a single observed instance of behaviour.

misconceptions.label: Ignoring situational factors
misconceptions.description: Explaining behaviour entirely in terms of a person's character while overlooking plausible circumstances that could equally explain it.

misconceptions.label: Confirmation bias
misconceptions.description: Treating evidence as confirming an existing suspicion while not seeking or weighing evidence that could point elsewhere.

misconceptions.label: Ignoring alternative explanations
misconceptions.description: Settling on one explanation for behaviour without having generated or considered any plausible alternative.

misconceptions.label: Skipping the covariation check
misconceptions.description: Explaining behaviour with a trait without checking consistency, distinctiveness or consensus first.

misconceptions.label: Ignoring the base rate
misconceptions.description: Letting a vivid specific case override how common that kind of case generally is.

misconceptions.label: Regression misattributed as an effect
misconceptions.description: Crediting an intervention for a change that ordinary regression to the mean would predict anyway.

misconceptions.label: Small-sample overconfidence
misconceptions.description: Treating a pattern seen in only a few instances as if it were as reliable as one seen across many.

misconceptions.label: A words/nonverbal mismatch ignored
misconceptions.description: Taking someone's stated words at face value when their tone or nonverbal behaviour conflicts with them, without noting the mismatch itself as worth attention.

misconceptions.label: Tone and pacing ignored
misconceptions.description: Attending only to the literal content of what someone says while ignoring what their tone, pace, or delivery itself communicates.

misconceptions.label: No baseline established
misconceptions.description: Treating a behaviour as significant or unusual without first knowing what's normal for that specific person.

misconceptions.label: Signal meaning assumed universal
misconceptions.description: Assuming a gesture, expression, or behaviour means the same thing regardless of the person, context, or culture it occurs in.

misconceptions.label: A single cue over-read
misconceptions.description: Treating one isolated signal as if it definitively reveals someone's emotion or intent, without considering context or alternative causes.

misconceptions.label: A physiological cause mistaken for an emotional one
misconceptions.description: Attributing a physical response — caused by caffeine, tiredness, temperature, illness — to an emotional state without considering the physical explanation.

misconceptions.label: Group energy misread from one person
misconceptions.description: Judging an entire group's mood or engagement from one person's visible reaction, rather than the pattern across the group.

misconceptions.label: An inferred read acted on without checking
misconceptions.description: Acting on an inferred read of someone's internal state as if it were confirmed, without ever checking it against reality through a direct, low-pressure question.

misconceptions.label: Half-listening
misconceptions.description: Appearing to listen while mentally elsewhere — distracted, or already planning what to say next — rather than actually taking in what's being said.

misconceptions.label: Paraphrasing skipped
misconceptions.description: Moving straight to your own response or opinion without first confirming you've understood what the other person actually said.

misconceptions.label: A leading question used instead of an open one
misconceptions.description: Asking a question that presupposes or steers toward a particular answer, rather than one that genuinely opens space for the other person's actual view.

misconceptions.label: Listening to rebut, not to understand
misconceptions.description: Mentally formulating a counter-argument or response while the other person is still speaking, instead of actually taking in what they're saying.

misconceptions.label: Solutions offered when not asked for
misconceptions.description: Jumping to solve a problem when the person wanted to be heard, not have the problem fixed for them.

misconceptions.label: What's unsaid missed
misconceptions.description: Focusing only on what's explicitly said, missing hesitations, omissions, or a topic being noticeably avoided.

misconceptions.label: A gap filled with assumption instead of a question
misconceptions.description: Filling a genuine gap in understanding with an assumption, rather than simply asking a clarifying question.

misconceptions.label: Own communication style assumed universal
misconceptions.description: Listening and interpreting through your own default communication style or norms, without adjusting for someone whose style genuinely differs.

misconceptions.label: Feedback given as a vague trait or judgment
misconceptions.description: Giving feedback as a general trait or character judgment ("you're disorganized") rather than a specific, observed behavior the person can actually act on.

misconceptions.label: The person's character labeled, not the action
misconceptions.description: Critiquing who someone is as a person, rather than a specific action they took, even when the intent was to address the action.

misconceptions.label: Feedback delivered as an ambush
misconceptions.description: Giving feedback at a poorly chosen time or in a way that catches the person off guard, publicly or without warning, rather than framing it so it can actually be heard.

misconceptions.label: Feedback unbalanced — all criticism or empty praise
misconceptions.description: Giving feedback that's either all corrective with no acknowledgment of what's working, or all praise with no honest corrective content — either way failing to give an accurate, useful picture.

misconceptions.label: Immediate defensive justification
misconceptions.description: Responding to feedback by immediately justifying or explaining it away, before actually taking in what was said.

misconceptions.label: Feedback treated as an attack on identity
misconceptions.description: Treating critical feedback about a specific action as a judgment on one's fundamental worth or identity, rather than information about one instance of behavior.

misconceptions.label: Vague feedback accepted without asking for specifics
misconceptions.description: Accepting vague, hard-to-act-on feedback at face value without asking what specifically it refers to.

misconceptions.label: All feedback treated as equally valid
misconceptions.description: Treating every piece of feedback received as equally valid and actionable, regardless of the source's expertise, context, or pattern of repetition.

misconceptions.label: Your own view projected onto someone else
misconceptions.description: Assuming someone else sees a situation the way you do, rather than actually imagining their distinct, possibly different, actual view.

misconceptions.label: A knowledge asymmetry ignored
misconceptions.description: Failing to account for what the other person does or doesn't know that you do (or vice versa), and judging their reaction as if they had your full information.

misconceptions.label: Only the cognitive view considered, not the emotional one
misconceptions.description: Working out what someone likely thinks about a situation while ignoring how it likely feels to them — treating perspective-taking as purely an information problem.

misconceptions.label: An empathic guess treated as confirmed without checking
misconceptions.description: Treating your inferred read of someone's perspective or feelings as established fact, without checking it against what they actually say.

misconceptions.label: Agreement treated as required to validate
misconceptions.description: Believing that acknowledging someone's perspective as understandable requires actually agreeing with their conclusion or decision.

misconceptions.label: Empathic engagement overextended past a sustainable limit
misconceptions.description: Continuing to extend full empathic engagement past the point that's sustainable, without recognizing or setting a reasonable limit.

misconceptions.label: Perspective-taking abandoned once disagreement starts
misconceptions.description: Dropping any attempt to understand the other person's view as soon as a disagreement becomes heated, rather than maintaining it alongside holding your own position.

misconceptions.label: Honesty and care treated as a tradeoff
misconceptions.description: Treating directness and care as mutually exclusive — assuming that being honest requires sacrificing care, or that being caring requires softening the truth.

misconceptions.label: A single impressive gesture overweighted as proof of trustworthiness
misconceptions.description: Treating one impressive or generous gesture as strong evidence of trustworthiness, while discounting the slower, less visible pattern of predictable follow-through that actually builds trust over time.

misconceptions.label: Self-disclosure mismatched to the relationship's actual pace
misconceptions.description: Sharing personal information either far ahead of or far behind what the relationship's actual closeness and reciprocity would call for, rather than matching disclosure to the relationship's actual pace.

misconceptions.label: Trust extended based on likability rather than track record
misconceptions.description: Extending a significant degree of trust to someone based on how likable or charismatic they are, rather than on their actual demonstrated track record of follow-through.

misconceptions.label: An apology treated as sufficient to repair broken trust
misconceptions.description: Treating a verbal apology alone as sufficient to repair trust after a breach, without the sustained, consistent follow-through that actually rebuilds it over time.
